messages.subject: interns and projects
parts:
Ben said (in the context of using sympy to evaluate
the Jacobians we've been calculating):
> A decent undergraduate mathy project might be to write Python scripts verifying all of stan's derivatives.

That would be a nice project and I just verified that
it's dead easy.

We could also use help building more models. That would
require more stats background.

We just missed the March 9 deadline for Google's Summer of
Code 2012. I'd heard of it, but hadn't been thinking of it

We should keep it in mind for next year. I saw a link
from Sympy, which is why I just went to check it out.

- Bob

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: interns and projects
parts:
On Tuesday, March 20, 2012 3:47:35 AM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
Ben said (in the context of using sympy to evaluate
the Jacobians we've been calculating):
 > A decent undergraduate mathy project might be to write Python scripts verifying all of stan's derivatives.

That would be a nice project and I just verified that
it's dead easy.

One thing is that sympy does not have many distributions (maybe just normal or uniform) or much of anything related to statistics. So, part of a project that might also be useful to sympy would be to contribute a bunch of PDFs and CDFs to lay the groundwork for verifying the derivatives of a PDF wrt the primitive parameters stan uses. A more ambitious undertaking might be to make it so that expressions could be simplified into summation notation instead of these giant strings we get by just transforming a few parameters.

We could also use help building more models.  That would
require more stats background.

We just missed the March 9 deadline for Google's Summer of
Code 2012.  I'd heard of it, but hadn't been thinking of it

Google Summer of Code for 2013+ is a good opportunity, but it is very competitive. We would really need to start preparing a few months in advance to outline some projects that are feasible for an undergraduate to do in (less than) a summer. For example, the sagemath project (which is much more extensive than stan) just got a GSOC position after several years of applying and now they are in the process of figuring out which students to match with which projects. They have a mailing list

https://groups.google.com/forum/?fromgroups#!forum/sage-gsoc

and a wiki

http://wiki.sagemath.org/GSoC

Although Google might well be interested in funding work on stan, a successful GSOC application requires a lot of organization.

Ben
